report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Improving LLM preference prediction by averaging two perspectives

text.text: People often seek advice when choosing a film, a book, or another experience whose value depends on their tastes.
Large language models (LLMs) provide a convenient way to obtain such advice.
We test a simple method for improving their predictions, inspired by the wisdom of the inner crowd.
An LLM first predicts a person's movie rating from that person's past ratings.
It then predicts how the general public, given the same history, would predict the same person's rating.
Averaging takes the arithmetic mean of these two responses.
We evaluated 12 GPT model snapshots using MovieLens 1M.
A history-size study tested 1-20 ratings for 55 users and extended the comparison to 55 ratings for 32 eligible users.
Averaging improved mean squared error relative to the first response even at the longest history.
A subsequent evaluation used 10 target films per person with 10 fixed history ratings.
Across 320 user-movie pairs, mean squared error was 1.218 for the first response, 1.147 for the public-perspective response, and 1.150 for Averaging.
Additional analyses showed that Averaging reduced errors of at least 1.5 rating points, whereas the first response produced more exact matches.
These advantages did not extend to every error threshold or metric.
The findings connect inner-crowd research with a simple conversational method for preference prediction and show why the choice of response should reflect the prediction objective.
Which film should we watch tonight?
Will a friend enjoy the book we plan to give them?
Such questions require predictions about preferences.
There is no universally correct film or book: the same experience can delight one person and disappoint another.
Yet people have information that may help them choose well.
They remember past experiences, observe other people's choices, and ask for advice.
Research on matters of taste examines how these sources of information help people anticipate what they will enjoy (Yaniv et al., 2011; Müller-Trede et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Research on matters of taste examines how these sources of information help people anticipate what they will enjoy <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Yaniv et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Müller-Trede et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Using that information is not straightforward.

People can overestimate how well their friends know their preferences, and familiarity with a partner does not ensure accurate predictions of that partner's tastes (Gershoff & Johar, 2006; Lerouge & Warlop, 2006).
text.formatted: People can overestimate how well their friends know their preferences, and familiarity with a partner does not ensure accurate predictions of that partner's tastes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Gershoff & Johar, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Lerouge & Warlop, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, another person's reported experience can be informative even when the person is unfamiliar.
Studies of affective forecasting show that others' reactions can improve predictions of one's own reactions, although people may underestimate their value (Gilbert et al., 2009; Walsh & Ayton, 2009).
text.formatted: Studies of affective forecasting show that others' reactions can improve predictions of one's own reactions, although people may underestimate their value <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gilbert et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Walsh & Ayton, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: A stranger's opinion can sometimes be as useful as a friend's (Eggleston et al., 2015).
text.formatted: A stranger's opinion can sometimes be as useful as a friend's <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Eggleston et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, knowing someone well and knowing how to use an opinion are different problems.

Previous choices also reveal information about whose opinions will be useful. Yaniv et al. (2011) showed that reliance on similar advisers and majority opinions depends on taste discrimination. Gershman et al. (2017) further showed that people infer latent groups from observed choices and use this structure to decide whom to follow.

(2017)</ref> further showed that people infer latent groups from observed choices and use this structure to decide whom to follow.

text.text: This process goes beyond comparing two people's choices in isolation.

Preference research also examines when dissimilar opinions can inform prediction (Fujisaki & Yang, 2025) and, in ongoing work, whether response time can help select a single aesthetic judgment to represent a crowd (Fujisaki, in preparation).
text.formatted: Preference research also examines when dissimilar opinions can inform prediction <ref type="bibr">(Fujisaki & Yang, 2025)</ref> and, in ongoing work, whether response time can help select a single aesthetic judgment to represent a crowd <ref type="bibr">(Fujisaki, in preparation)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these approaches ask how information about a person, an adviser, or a judgment can make advice more useful.
The degree of shared taste also varies across aesthetic domains (Vessel et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The degree of shared taste also varies across aesthetic domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Vessel et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: LLMs provide a new interface for this everyday problem.
A person can list films they liked and disliked and ask whether they would enjoy another film.

Studies have examined recommendation through natural-language prompts, including rating prediction and the ranking of candidate items (Liu et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023). Kang et al. (2023) directly tested whether LLMs can predict an unknown rating from a user's previous ratings.

(2023)</ref> directly tested whether LLMs can predict an unknown rating from a user's previous ratings.

text.text: Their work establishes the feasibility of the task while showing that pretrained models can lag behind collaborative-filtering approaches.
Fluency in discussing a film therefore does not establish accurate personalization.
Here we ask whether a small change in the conversation can improve the prediction made from the information already supplied.
Our approach draws on the wisdom of the inner crowd.
Several estimates from one person can contain useful information beyond a single estimate.
Averaging them can therefore improve accuracy, even without consulting another person (Vul & Pashler, 2008; Herzog & Hertwig, 2009 , 2014a).
text.formatted: Averaging them can therefore improve accuracy, even without consulting another person <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Vul & Pashler, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Herzog & Hertwig, 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">, 2014a)</ref>.

text.text: Research has examined how this benefit depends on memory, repeated sampling, and the interval between judgments, using both laboratory tasks and large natural experiments (Hourihan & Benjamin, 2010; Rauhut & Lorenz, 2011; Steegen et al., 2014; van Dolder & van den Assem, 2018).

text.text: The benefit varies with the questions, the judge's expertise, and the way the second estimate is elicited (Müller-Trede, 2011; Fiechter & Kornell, 2021; Gaertig & Simmons, 2021).

text.text: An inner crowd is therefore a procedure for making better use of available judgments, rather than a guarantee that any second answer will help.
Generating judgments and deciding what to do with them are also distinct steps.
People do not always recognize when combining their own estimates would be useful (Fraundorf & Benjamin, 2014; Herzog & Hertwig, 2014b).
text.formatted: People do not always recognize when combining their own estimates would be useful <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Fraundorf & Benjamin, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Herzog & Hertwig, 2014b)</ref>.

text.text: Research comparing averaging with the selection of a single confidence judgment similarly shows why the evaluation criterion matters (Litvinova et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Research comparing averaging with the selection of a single confidence judgment similarly shows why the evaluation criterion matters <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Litvinova et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The approach extends beyond factual estimation. Barneron et al. (2019) found benefits from combining repeated essay evaluations by the same rater.

text.text: This suggests that repeated judgments can improve evaluation even when the task involves subjective assessment. Fujisaki et al. (2022) made the connection to matters of taste directly.

text.text: Participants rated paintings or music from their own perspective and estimated how much the public would like the same items.
Averaging these two ratings improved the prediction of other participants' preferences relative to using the participant's own rating.
Averaging also outperformed the public estimate for paintings; the corresponding difference was not established for music.
This procedure offers a simple way to obtain a more informative judgment from one adviser.
Its central idea is to elicit another perspective and combine the resulting responses.
A related possibility now exists within an LLM. Chuang et al. (2025) showed that aggregating multiple responses from a model can improve numerical guesstimation.
text.formatted: A related possibility now exists within an LLM. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Chuang et al. (2025)</ref> showed that aggregating multiple responses from a model can improve numerical guesstimation.

text.text: Their work links LLM decoding to crowd wisdom in tasks involving quantities and forecasts.
The present study examines individual preferences and elicits two responses through different instructions.
First, the model predicts a target person's rating from that person's history.
Second, it estimates how the public, seeing the same history, would predict that same person's rating.
We compare the first response (R1), the second response (R²), and their arithmetic mean (Averaging).
Throughout, the target remains one person's rating of one film.
We first varied the number of history ratings, from 1 to 55, to test whether the method remained useful as information about the person increased.
We then predicted 10 films per person using a fixed history of 10 ratings.
This second study broadens the test beyond a single selected film.
The main analyses concern mean squared error (MSE).
Additional analyses examine mean absolute error (MAE), exact matches, and the differences between R² and Averaging.
This order separates the basic improvement over a direct prediction from the further question of which response is most useful for a particular purpose.
>Method and results
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Method and results</head>

text.text: Figure 1 illustrates the basic procedure.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> illustrates the basic procedure.

text.text: For each prediction, the model received a target user's previous movie ratings, the corresponding titles and genres, and the title and genres of a target movie.
It then produced two predictions about the same target rating.
All history ratings preceded the target rating, which was hidden.
R1 asked for a direct prediction of the target user's rating.
R² was generated in the same conversation after the model's complete R1 response.
It retained the same history and R1 response, then asked how members of the public would predict the same user's rating from that information.
It requested the mean of these imagined predictions.
The question concerned the public's prediction about this user, not the public's own liking of the movie.
Both responses could use decimals from 1 to 5.
Averaging was calculated as (R1 + R²) / 2, with no fitted weights.
We used MovieLens 1M, which contains actual movie ratings on an integer scale from 1 to 5 (Harper & Konstan, 2015).
text.formatted: We used MovieLens 1M, which contains actual movie ratings on an integer scale from 1 to 5 <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Harper & Konstan, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: MovieLens has also been used to study variation in recommendation accuracy across users (Analytis & Hager, 2023) and to evaluate LLM prediction of user ratings (Kang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: MovieLens has also been used to study variation in recommendation accuracy across users <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Analytis & Hager, 2023)</ref> and to evaluate LLM prediction of user ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It allows us to assess predictions against an observed preference, rather than an investigator's judgment of whether a recommendation seems appropriate.
We evaluated 12 fixed GPT model snapshots.
Each user-film-model combination started with a fresh context.
The model received no outcome feedback, and predictions were not exchanged across models or films.
No model was fine-tuned; history size refers to the examples included in the prompt.
We first calculated each model's squared prediction error, then averaged errors across models and users.
Thus, the main analysis describes individual-model performance.
It is distinct from first averaging predictions across 12 models.
Paired confidence intervals resampled users 10,000 times, keeping their model and condition observations together.
Detailed settings and sampling rules appear in Appendix A; the original prompts appear in Appendix B.

text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: Two perspectives on one prediction target.
An LLM receives a target user's past ratings and information about a target movie.
R1 directly predicts that user's rating.
R² estimates how the general public, given the same history, would predict the same user's rating of the same movie; it does not estimate the public's own liking of that movie.
R² is generated in the same conversation after the complete R1 response.
Averaging is the arithmetic mean, (R1 + R²) / 2.
Each prediction is evaluated against the target user's held-out MovieLens rating, which is not supplied to the model.
The numerical values are illustrative.
The first study used one target film per person and nested histories of 1, 3, 5, 10, and 20 ratings.
Of 56 sampled users, 55 had complete responses in every condition.
For these users, the person, target film, and true rating were fixed across history sizes.
All three methods improved as history increased (Figure 2A).
text.formatted: All three methods improved as history increased (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2A</ref>).

text.text: From one to 20 ratings, MSE fell from 1.688 to 0.838 for R1, from 1.331 to 0.831 for R², and from 1.460 to 0.804 for Averaging.
R² had the lowest MSE with one, three, or five history ratings.
Averaging had the lowest MSE with 10 or 20 ratings.
The benefit of Averaging over R1 was larger when little history was available.
The MSE reduction was 0.228 at one rating, 95% CI [0.117, 0.349], and 0.034 at 20 ratings, [-0.009, 0.074].
The change in this benefit was -0.194, [-0.322, -0.078].
Additional information therefore reduced the initial advantage of Averaging.
A constant prediction of 3 had MSE 1.945, higher than every method at every tested history size.
We next extended the history to 55 ratings for the 32 users who had sufficient earlier ratings for their original target.
The comparison used these same users at every history size (Figure 2B).
text.formatted: The comparison used these same users at every history size (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2B</ref>).

text.text: At 55 ratings, MSE was 0.976 for R1, 0.892 for R², and 0.910 for Averaging.
R² reduced MSE relative to R1 by 0.085, 95% CI [0.006, 0.170].
Averaging reduced it by 0.067, [0.026, 0.110].
R² had the lowest point estimate at all six history sizes in this subset.
Thus, the usefulness of a second prediction remained at the longest history tested.
The two samples must be kept distinct.
At 20 ratings, Averaging ranked first in the full 55-user sample, whereas R² ranked first in the 32-user subset.
Moreover, the change in the Averaging benefit between 20 and 55 ratings was uncertain, -0.008, 95% CI [-0.057, 0.043].
The results show persistence with longer histories; they do not establish a constant benefit across history sizes or users.
The second study tested whether the result depended on the single target initially selected for each person.
We retained the 32 users and predicted 10 films for each, using 10 fixed history ratings per user.
The target set included the original film and nine additional eligible films.
All predictions were newly generated.
This gave 320 user-movie pairs covering 284 distinct movies and 7,680 valid model responses, with no missing responses.
Each film was predicted in a separate conversation from the same history.
Both R² and Averaging improved MSE relative to R1 (Figure 3; Table 1).
text.formatted: Both R² and Averaging improved MSE relative to R1 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Across 3,840 predictions per method, MSE was 1.218 for R1, 1.147 for R², and 1.150 for Averaging.
The reduction relative to R1 was 0.071 for R², 95% CI [0.018, 0.125], and 0.067 for Averaging, [0.039, 0.096].
At the user level, Averaging improved MSE for 25 of the 32 users.
The improvement therefore extended beyond the original one-film task.
The originally selected films were easier in the observed data: R1 MSE was 0.950 for the original targets and 1.248 for the nine added targets.
Nevertheless, the MSE benefit of Averaging over R1 was almost identical, 0.0673 and 0.0674, respectively.
The intervals for the original-versus-added differences included zero.
These results support the broader ten-film evaluation while cautioning against treating the initial one-film errors as stable properties of individual users.
